spans.text: The E form's empty fret cost nothing, because it sat right at the edge, where the window was already ending. Here it lands in the middle: two frets of dots, a dead fret, then two more frets of dots. That's why this window doesn't settle under one hand the way most of the others do — it's the shape talking, not your reach. Chapter 3 already said the pentatonic version of this window asked for a stretch or a shift; the reason was always this hole, it just wasn't visible until every fret in the window had a name.

Chapter 3 called this the widest window of the five, and at the pentatonic layer it was. It no longer is: three of the five windows now span five frets, so width alone doesn't set the D form apart anymore. What does is the gap running through the middle of it — the only window in this chapter with a hole in the shape rather than at its edge.

Nothing about that makes the window worse — it makes it the one that asks for the most planning. Run it carelessly and it sounds restless; the two roots are worth knowing cold before you improvise here.

Chapter 1 lit two roots in this window. Chapter 2 filled it with seven chord tones. Chapter 3 brought it to twelve. It now holds all seventeen — the whole scale, complete — and that closes out the fifth and last of the five windows this chapter fills in.
What's left is putting the five back together.
